chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl, who said:
I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about the people’s saying in congregational salat (prayer), when Fātiḥat al-Kitāb is recited, “Āmīn.” He said: “How good it is, and lower the voice with it.”

So the first thing concerning this report is that its narrator is Jamīl, and he has narrated the opposite of that, namely what we have presented earlier from his statement: “Do not say Āmīn; rather say: al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi al-ʿālamīn.” When he has narrated what contradicts this narration and agrees with the narration of others, then acting upon that is necessary instead of the other. And even if it were accepted, it would be possible to interpret it as a form of taqiyyah, due to the consensus of the rightful sect upon abandoning acting by it; and also, indeed...

key_terms.آمِينَ: Āmīn, the expression said after recitation
key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary conformity under specific circumstances
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), the ritual act under discussion
key_terms.الطَّائِفَةِ الْمُحِقَّةِ: the rightful sect, referring to the Shia community
key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ: the opening phrase of al-Fātiḥah, cited here as the alternative utterance
key_terms.جَمَاعَةً: in congregation, indicating communal performance of salat (prayer)
key_terms.فَاتِحَةُ الْكِتَابِ: the Opening of the Book, meaning Sūrat al-Fātiḥah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on saying Āmīn after al-Ḥamd in congregational salat (prayer) according to al-Istibṣār?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling of saying “Āmīn” after Sūrat al-Fātiḥah in congregational salat (prayer). The compiler then rejects acting upon this narration because the same narrator transmitted a contradictory report, and he further states that, if accepted, it may be understood as taqiyyah in light of the consensus of the Shia community.
